scenes.label: Extinct Felid Genus
scenes.line: Smilodon is a genus of extinct felids and one of the best-known saber-toothed predators and prehistoric mammals. Smilodon lived in the Americas during the Pleistocene to early Holocene epoch, spanning from 2.5 million to at latest 8,200 years ago.
scenes.image_prompt: Ancient fossilized skeletal remains of a large prehistoric predator resting inside a dark museum display case., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: First Naming
scenes.line: The genus was named in 1842 based on fossils recovered from Brazil. The generic name means scalpel or two-edged knife combined with tooth.
scenes.image_prompt: A collection of weathered stone tools and old fossils resting on a wooden table inside an archive., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Three Recognized Species
scenes.line: Three species are recognized today: S. gracilis, S. fatalis, and S. populator. The two latter species were probably descended from S. gracilis, which itself probably evolved from Megantereon.
scenes.image_prompt: Three distinct rock formations standing side by side in a rugged, arid desert valley., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: La Brea Tar Pits
scenes.line: The hundreds of specimens obtained from the La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles constitute the largest collection of Smilodon fossils. Overall, Smilodon was more robustly built than any extant cat, with particularly well-developed forelimbs and exceptionally long upper canine teeth.
scenes.image_prompt: A bubbling asphalt pool surrounded by green trees and urban park grass in daylight., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Jaw Gape
scenes.line: Its jaw had a bigger gape than that of modern cats, and its upper canines were slender and fragile, being adapted for precision killing. S. gracilis was the smallest species at 55 to 100 kg in weight.
scenes.image_prompt: The skeletal jawbone of a large animal mounted on a black metal display stand., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Fatalis Dimensions
scenes.line: S. fatalis had a weight of 160 to 280 kg and height of 100 cm and body length of 175 cm. Both of these species are mainly known from North America, but remains from South America have also been attributed to them.
scenes.image_prompt: An open expanse of grassy plains with scattered acacia trees under a bright afternoon sun., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Largest Species Populator
scenes.line: S. populator from South America was the largest species, at 220 to 470 kg in weight and 120 cm in height. The coat pattern of Smilodon is unknown, but it has been artistically restored with plain or spotted patterns.
scenes.image_prompt: A massive boulder resting on a grassy plateau overlooking a wide river valley., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: North American Prey
scenes.line: In North America, Smilodon hunted large herbivores such as bison and camels. It remained successful even when encountering new prey taxa in South America such as Macrauchenia and ground sloths.
scenes.image_prompt: An empty grassy meadow where large herds once roamed under a vast sky., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Killed By Holding
scenes.line: Smilodon is thought to have killed its prey by holding it still with its forelimbs and biting it, but in what manner the bite itself was delivered is unclear. Scientists debate whether Smilodon had a social or a solitary lifestyle.
scenes.image_prompt: A strong, thick tree trunk gripped tightly by heavy, gnarled roots., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Closed Habitats
scenes.line: Smilodon probably lived in relatively closed habitats such as forests and bush, which would have provided cover for ambushing prey. S. populator has been suggested to have hunted in open terrain.
scenes.image_prompt: A thick, overgrown forest thicket with dense bushes and shadowy pathways., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: End Pleistocene Extinction
scenes.line: Smilodon died out as part of the end-Pleistocene extinction event, which occurred around 13,000 to 9,000 years ago. Its reliance on large animals has been proposed as the cause of its extinction.
scenes.image_prompt: A barren, dusty landscape under a heavy, overcast twilight sky., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Habitat Turnover
scenes.line: Smilodon may have been impacted by habitat turnover and loss of prey on which it specialized due to possible climatic impacts. Other factors include the effects of recently arrived humans on prey populations and other environmental changes.
scenes.image_prompt: A dead tree standing in a dry, cracked mud flat under a glaring sun., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Lund Fossils in Caves
scenes.line: During the 1830s, Danish naturalist Peter Wilhelm Lund and his assistants collected fossils in the calcareous caves near Lagoa Santa, Brazil. Among the thousands of fossils found, he recognized a few isolated cheek teeth as belonging to a hyena, which he named Hyaena neogaea in 1839.

scenes.label: Distinct Genus Conclusion
scenes.line: After more material was found, Lund concluded the fossils instead belonged to a distinct genus of felids, though transitional to the hyenas. He stated it would have matched the largest modern predators in size, and was more robust than any modern cat.
scenes.image_prompt: A collection of assorted animal bone fragments laid out in rows on a laboratory table., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Naming Populator
scenes.line: Realizing his first choice was taken, he instead named it Smilodon populator in 1842. He explained the species name populator as the destroyer, which has also been translated as he who brings devastation.
scenes.image_prompt: An old, leather-bound scientific ledger opened to a handwritten page with faded ink., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Canines Found Later
scenes.line: Lund based the name on the shape of the incisors, and the large canine teeth were not known until 1846. By 1846, Lund had acquired nearly every part of the skeleton from different individuals.
scenes.image_prompt: A single curved fossil fragment illuminated by a focused desk lamp in a dark room., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Invalid Neogaea Name
scenes.line: Though some later authors used Lund's original species name neogaea instead of populator, it is now considered an invalid nomen nudum. Some South American specimens have been referred to other genera, but these are now thought to be junior synonyms of S. populator.
scenes.image_prompt: A red ink cross drawn over a line of text on an old parchment document., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Texas Discovery
scenes.line: In 1869, American paleontologist Joseph Leidy described a maxilla fragment with a molar discovered in a petroleum bed in Hardin County, Texas. He referred the specimen to the genus Felis, but found it distinct enough for its own subgenus, giving the species name meaning deadly.
scenes.image_prompt: Dark, viscous crude oil seeping slowly through sandy soil near a riverbank., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Cope Combination
scenes.line: In an 1880 article, American paleontologist Edward Drinker Cope pointed out that the molar was identical to that of Smilodon. Most North American finds were scanty until excavations began in the La Brea Tar Pits, where hundreds of individuals of S. fatalis have been found since 1875.
scenes.image_prompt: A pair of antique brass reading glasses resting on top of an open scientific textbook., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Taxonomy Debate
scenes.line: American paleontologist Annalisa Berta considered the holotype of S. fatalis too incomplete to be an adequate type specimen. Nordic paleontologists Björn Kurtén and Lars Werdelin supported the distinctness of the two species in an article published in 1990.
scenes.image_prompt: A magnifying glass hovering over a cracked and fragmented piece of old bone., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: California State Fossil
scenes.line: One of the most famous of prehistoric mammals, Smilodon has often been featured in popular media and is the state fossil of California. The term saber-tooth itself refers to an ecomorph consisting of various groups of extinct predatory synapsids.
scenes.image_prompt: A large stone monument plaque mounted on a rough rock wall in a public park., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Tribes of Machairodontinae
scenes.line: Within the family Felidae, machairodonts are divided into three tribes: Metailurini, Homotherini, and Smilodontini. Members of Smilodontini are defined by their long slender canines with fine to no serrations.
scenes.image_prompt: Three smooth river stones resting in a neat row on a sandy riverbank., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Divergence Timing
scenes.line: The ancestors of living cats and Machairodontinae are estimated to have diverged around 20 million years ago. The earliest felids are known from the Oligocene of Europe, and the earliest one with saber-tooth features is the Miocene genus Pseudaelurus.
scenes.image_prompt: A gnarled tree root system branching out across the forest floor in different directions., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Skull Morphology
scenes.line: The skull and mandible morphology of the earliest saber-toothed cats was similar to that of modern clouded leopards. Machairodonts once represented a dominant group distributed across Africa, Eurasia and North America, but progressively declined over the course of the Pleistocene.

scenes.label: Climate Variation
scenes.line: S. fatalis size varies based on the climate, with the species reaching larger sizes during warmer periods. Despite the large number of remains found, no baculum, or penis bone, has yet been found for Smilodon.
scenes.image_prompt: Dense green foliage thriving under bright, warm rays of sunlight breaking through clouds., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Final Restoration Consensus
scenes.line: A 2022 study concluded that the upper canines of Smilodon would have been visible when the mouth was closed. Phylogenetic analysis recovered Smilodon as a diurnal predator in ancient habitats.
scenes.image_prompt: A detailed paleontological illustration resting flat on a wooden drafting table., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Hyoid Bones
scenes.line: S. fatalis had proportionally larger hyoid bones than modern felid species and thus likely produced deeper vocalizations. While Smilodon had the same number of hyoid bones as the roaring cats, their shape was closer to that of purring species.
scenes.image_prompt: Close up of an animal skull resting on the forest floor among dry leaves., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Brain Patterns
scenes.line: The brain of Smilodon had sulcal patterns similar to modern cats, which suggests an increased complexity of the regions that control the sense of hearing, sight, and coordination of the limbs. Felid saber-tooths in general had relatively small eyes that were not as forward-facing as those of modern cats, which have good binocular vision to help them move in trees.
scenes.image_prompt: A researcher in a bright laboratory examining fossil specimens with specialized tools., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Olfactory Receptors
scenes.line: By finding of correlation between relative cribriform plate size and repertoire of functional olfactory receptor genes, it was found that S. fatalis had a slightly smaller repertoire than modern felids with 600 olfatory receptor genes, compared to 677 of a domestic cat. This indicates that S. fatalis used less olfaction for its daily activities than modern felids.
scenes.image_prompt: Scientific instruments resting beside handwritten notes and open reference books on a desk., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Ambush Predator
scenes.line: Smilodon was likely an ambush predator that concealed itself in dense vegetation, as its limb proportions were similar to modern forest-dwelling cats, and its short tail would not have helped it balance while running. Tracks from Argentina named Felipeda miramarensis in 2019 may have been produced by Smilodon.
scenes.image_prompt: Dense green undergrowth and tall grasses hiding the base of large forest trees., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Track Details
scenes.line: If correctly identified, the tracks indicate that the animal had fully retractible claws, plantigrade feet, lacked strong supination capabilities in its paws, notably robust forelimbs compared to the hindlimbs, and was probably an ambush predator. Unlike its ancestor Megantereon, which was at least partially scansorial and therefore able to climb trees, Smilodon was probably completely terrestrial due to its greater weight and lack of climbing adaptations.
scenes.image_prompt: A close up shot of a muddy riverbank with distinct preserved animal tracks., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Heel Bone
scenes.line: The heel bone of Smilodon was fairly long, which suggests it was a good jumper. Its well-developed flexor and extensor muscles in its forearms probably enabled it to pull down, and securely hold down, large prey.
scenes.image_prompt: A preserved calcaneus bone displayed inside a glass museum exhibit case., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Humeri Analysis
scenes.line: Analysis of the cross-sections of S. fatalis humeri indicated that they were strengthened by cortical thickening to such an extent that they would have been able to sustain greater loading than those of extant big cats, or of the extinct American lion. The humerus cortical wall in S. fatalis was a 15 % thicker than expected in modern big cats of similar size.
scenes.image_prompt: A cross section of a dense white bone showing thick outer cortical walls., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Femur Thickening
scenes.line: The thickening of S. fatalis femurs was within the range of extant felids. An apex predator, Smilodon primarily hunted large mammals.
scenes.image_prompt: A long leg bone specimen laid out on a dark padded examination table., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Tar Pits Isotopes
scenes.line: Isotopes preserved in the bones of S. fatalis in the La Brea Tar Pits reveal that ruminants like bison (Bison antiquus, which was much larger than the modern American bison) and camels (Camelops) were most commonly taken by the cats there. S. fatalis may have also occasionally preyed upon Glyptotherium, based on a skull from a juvenile G. texanum recovered from Pleistocene deposits in Arizona that bear the distinctive elliptical puncture marks best matching those of Smilodon, indicating that the predator successfully bit into the skull through the glyptodont's armored cephalic shield.
scenes.image_prompt: Dark bubbling asphalt pools surrounded by dry shrubs and scattered pale bones., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Florida Enamel
scenes.line: Isotopes preserved in the tooth enamel of S. gracilis specimens from Florida show that this species fed on the peccary Platygonus and the llama-like Hemiauchenia. Stable carbon isotope measurements of S. gracilis remains in Florida varied significantly between different sites and show that the species was flexible in its feeding habits.
scenes.image_prompt: Wet sandy soil and lush green vegetation in a humid subtropical wetland environment., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Glacial Overlap
scenes.line: During the glacials, S. gracilis has overlapping values with Edward’s wolf (Canis edwardii), suggesting greater levels of competition for grazing herbivores. In contrast, during interglacials S. gracilis preyed upon browsers and niche partitioned with Canis edwardii, who still preferred grazing prey.
scenes.image_prompt: Cold snowy landscape with sparse frozen ground under a pale winter sky., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Dental Microwear
scenes.line: Dental microwear shows a trend of S. gracilis consuming harder, tougher foods during glacials as compared to interglacials. This finding suggests that S. gracilis preyed more heavily on larger mixed feeders with tougher hides during glacials, in contrast to interglacials, in which S. gracilis preferred soft-skinned browsers.
scenes.image_prompt: A close up view of tiny microscopic scratch marks on a polished white tooth surface., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Rancho La Brea
scenes.line: Isotopic studies of dire wolf (Aenocyon dirus) and American lion (Panthera atrox) bones show an overlap with S. fatalis in prey in Rancho La Brea, which suggests that they were competitors. More detailed isotope analysis at Rancho La Brea however, indicated that Smilodon fatalis preferred forest-dwelling prey such as tapirs, deer and forest-dwelling bison as opposed to the dire wolves' preferences for prey inhabiting open areas such as grassland.
scenes.image_prompt: A fenced paleontological excavation site with exposed fossil beds in the earth., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: East Africa
scenes.line: The availability of prey in the Rancho La Brea area was likely comparable to modern East Africa. As Smilodon migrated to South America, its diet changed; bison were absent, the horses and proboscideans were different, and native ungulates such as toxodonts and litopterns were completely unfamiliar, yet S. populator thrived as well there as its relatives in North America.
scenes.image_prompt: An open savannah plain featuring scattered trees and golden brown grasses., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Regressions
scenes.line: Regressions suggests that a 436 kg (961 lb) S. populator is capable of taking on prey up to 3 t (3.0 long tons; 3.3 short tons) with a pack of S. populator potentially being capable of taking down fully grown megaherbivores such as Megatherium and Notiomastodon. Isotopic analysis of the Pampean region suggests S. populator hunted in open C3/C4 areas and its main prey included ground sloths such as Lestodon and Megatherium, the equine Hippidion, and the camel-like litoptern ungulate Macrauchenia.
scenes.image_prompt: Large massive bones laid out in a row on the floor of a large warehouse., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Sergipe State
scenes.line: Within the Poço Redondo, Sergipe state of the Brazilian Intertropical Region, the main prey of S. populator consisted of rhinoceros-like ungulate Toxodon platensis, the large armadillo relatives Pachyarmatherium, Holmesina, species of the glyptodont genus Panochthus, the llama Palaeolama, the ground sloth Catonyx, and the equine Equus neogeus, and the crocodilian Caiman latirostris. This analysis of its diet also indicates that S. populator hunted both in open and forested habitats within the Brazilian Intertropical Region.
scenes.image_prompt: A humid tropical riverbank surrounded by thick vegetation and muddy banks., cinematic documentary style, dramatic lighting, photorealistic details, 8k resolution, National Geographic photography, moody atmosphere

scenes.label: Detailed Analysis
scenes.line: However, a more detailed analysis found the main prey of S. populator within the Brazilian Intertropical Region mainly predated upon Nothrotherium maquinense. The differences between the North and South American species may be due to the difference in prey between the two continents.

scenes.label: Frozen Discovery
scenes.line: The woolly mammoth lived from the Middle Pleistocene until its extinction in the Holocene epoch. Mammoth remains were long known in Asia before they became known to Europeans.

scenes.label: Legendary Explanations
scenes.line: The origin of these remains was long debated and often explained as the remains of legendary creatures. The mammoth was identified as an extinct elephant species by Georges Cuvier in 1796.

scenes.label: Fossil Examination
scenes.line: The first woolly mammoth remains studied by scientists were examined by the British physician Hans Sloane in 1728. Hans Sloane examined fossilised teeth and tusks from Siberia and was the first to recognise they belonged to elephants.

scenes.label: Biblical Floods

scenes.label: New Species
scenes.line: French biologist Georges Cuvier identified the woolly mammoth remains not as modern elephants, but as an entirely new species. The German naturalist Johann Friedrich Blumenbach gave the woolly mammoth its scientific name, Elephas primigenius, in 1799.

scenes.label: First Born

scenes.label: Word Origin
